summary: States requirements for a mechanism that identifies which name server instance answered a DNS query. With anycast and load balancing, many servers can share one address, making it hard to tell which one replied. A standard way to find out would help administrators with diagnostics. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Many helpers answer the same phone number. When something goes wrong, you want to know which helper picked up. This note says what a way to ask them should look like.

questions: how to tell which dns server answered
identify a dns name server instance
subtitle: Identifying which DNS server answered a query in anycast deployments

tldr.problem: When multiple DNS servers share one IP address through anycast or load balancing, administrators cannot easily tell which server answered a particular query, making diagnostics difficult.
tldr.mechanism: The document analyzes existing ad hoc mechanisms like BIND's HOSTNAME.BIND query and proposes requirements for a standardized way to identify a responding name server that does not require dedicated namespaces or compromise security.
tldr.outcome: This informational document catalogs advantages and disadvantages of the existing CHAOS class TXT RR mechanism and defines characteristics for an improved, implementation-neutral solution.

facts.label: Standard query
facts.value: HOSTNAME.BIND. in CHAOS class TXT RR

facts.label: Version query
facts.value: VERSION.BIND. in CHAOS class TXT RR

today: RFC 4892 remains an informational document that describes the problem and existing solution. A successor RFC, RFC 5001, later specified the DNS Name Server Identifier (NSID) Option as a standardized mechanism for server identification that addresses many of these requirements.

sections.title: The Problem: Identifying Name Servers
sections.content:
Determining which name server responds to a DNS query has become increasingly important as DNS deployments grow more complex. Anycast and load balancing allow multiple independent DNS servers to share a single IP address. This makes it impossible to identify which server answered a query using only the server's IP address, which was traditionally the simplest identification method.

In complex network topologies, administrators need to know which server is responding for diagnostics, performance monitoring, and troubleshooting. The problem is especially acute for authoritative nameservers that must serve hundreds of zones from a shared address.
sections.eli5: When many servers share one address, you need a special way to ask which one answered your question, not just which address it came from.

sections.title: Existing Conventions: The BIND Solution
sections.content:
Since the early days of BIND (Berkeley Internet Name Domain), a widespread convention has existed for server identification. A query for a TXT resource record in the CHAOS class (class 3) for the domain name HOSTNAME.BIND. returns a string configured by the administrator to uniquely identify that server. The default value is the result of the server's gethostname() system call.

A refinement to this mechanism, adopted by several vendors, uses ID.SERVER. instead of BIND.. For reference, the companion query VERSION.BIND. returns version information, though this is less widely implemented.

This mechanism is standards-compliant and uses the DNS protocol itself, which ensures identification goes to the same server as normal queries, bypassing firewall complications.
sections.eli5: You send a special DNS question asking 'What is your identity?' in a special language (CHAOS class), and the server answers with a name it was given.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
sections.content:
Advantages: The CHAOS/TXT mechanism stays within the DNS protocol itself, making it likely to reach the same server as normal queries. It requires no special firewall exceptions because it uses standard DNS. Configuration is simple for administrators, and the server operator has complete control over what information is disclosed, minimizing exposure of sensitive infrastructure details.

Disadvantages: The mechanism requires a second query to correlate results, which is unreliable in some network conditions. It reserves an entire DNS class (CHAOS) for essentially one zone, which is wasteful. The original form using BIND. is implementation-specific, making standardization inappropriate. There is no convention for what the response should contain or how to authenticate it. Finally, signing CHAOS class records with DNSSEC is impractical because each server must have a unique identity that cannot be signed by a shared key.
sections.eli5: The old way works, but it uses a special language only BIND speaks, wastes precious space, and there is no standard way to check if the answer is real.

sections.title: Requirements for a Better Solution
sections.content:
A superior mechanism should meet several characteristics. It must be in-band with DNS, allowing server identity to be part of a normal query or as a separate dedicated query. It should not require dedicated namespaces like the CHAOS class or the OPT pseudo-RR. It must be easy to implement and disable, with access controls available. Importantly, it should allow servers to return unique identifiers without exposing sensitive information like hostnames or private unicast IP addresses.

The mechanism should support authentication similar to DNSSEC, possibly through encryption options in the extension specification. Critically, it must be implementation-neutral, not tied to a particular DNS software like BIND. These requirements suggest a protocol extension that is cleaner than the current CHAOS-based approach while maintaining the same benefits of using DNS itself for identification.
sections.eli5: A new way should ask the question in regular DNS language, be easy for servers to answer, not leak secrets, and work the same for all DNS software.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
Providing identifying information about which server is responding creates potential security risks. An attacker could use this information to target specific servers with attacks, or to probe the infrastructure. The solution should allow operators to disable the functionality entirely or restrict who can query for it.

Server identification data must not be easily correlated with private hostnames or unicast IP addresses that operators consider sensitive. Additionally, propagating protocol or service metadata can expose DNS infrastructure to denial-of-service attacks, requiring extra care in solution design. Both authentication and confidentiality of identification data may be desirable: operators may wish to make such data available only to themselves and chosen associates, implying the need for both verification and privacy protection.
sections.eli5: Telling someone which server you are could help them attack you, so any new way needs built-in ways to keep this secret and prove the answer is real.
